name: Confucianism
line: Become humane through learning, good form and care for those nearest you.

quote.text: What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.

quotes.text: Is it not pleasant to learn with a constant perseverance and application?
When I walk along with two others, they may serve me as my teachers. I will select their good qualities and follow them, their bad qualities and avoid them.
When you know a thing, to hold that you know it; and when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it; this is knowledge.
When we see men of worth, we should think of equalling them; when we see men of a contrary character, we should turn inwards and examine ourselves.

At fifteen, I had my mind bent on learning. At thirty, I stood firm. At forty, I had no doubts. At fifty, I knew the decrees of Heaven. At sixty, my ear was an obedient organ for the reception of truth. At seventy, I could follow what my heart desired, without transgressing what was right.
The feeling of commiseration is the principle of benevolence.

words.usage: The central virtue. The character joins the signs for person and two: it exists only between people.
From court ceremony down to how you greet a neighbour. The shapes that let respect be seen.
The sense of what a situation requires of you, whatever it pays.
For Mencius, the fourth of the inborn sprouts of virtue.
The character shows a person standing by their word.
Care and respect for parents and ancestors. The character shows a child carrying an elder.
Paired with filial devotion as the root of all later virtue.
The heart held at the centre. Giving a task or a person your whole effort.

words.meaning: Reciprocity; putting yourself in another’s place
words.usage: Asked for one word to live by, Confucius chose this one.
Once a lord’s son. Confucius changed it to mean anyone of formed character, whatever their birth.
The one who thinks of gain where the exemplary person thinks of what is right.
The pull that a good character has on others, like the wind over grass.
For Confucians, the right path for people and for government, handed down from the early sage kings.
The moral order above human affairs. Confucius felt known by it when no one else understood him.
A ruler’s right to rule, which is kept by good government and lost by cruelty.
The first word of the Analects after the Master said. Study as the making of a person.
The inherited arts of poetry, music and ceremony that refine raw character.
Making words match realities. A ruler should rule and a father should act as a father.

words.meaning: The mean; staying centred in the ordinary
words.usage: Neither too much nor too little, held steady in daily affairs. Also the title of one of the Four Books.
Different things in good proportion, like flavours in a soup. It is the opposite of sameness.
Being inside what you appear to be outside.
The inner attitude that keeps ritual from being empty.
One organ that both thinks and feels. Chinese thought does not divide them.
Mencius called it good, Xunzi called it crooked, and the argument has never ended.
The perfected person. Confucius said he had never met one and was not one.

words.meaning: A scholar of the classics and rites
words.usage: The tradition’s own name for itself: the school of the Ru. Confucianism is a Western coinage.
Parent and child, ruler and minister, husband and wife, elder and younger, friend and friend.
Half of Confucius’s answer on humaneness: master yourself and return to good form.
Behaving in an empty room as you would before guests.
The first step of self-cultivation in the Great Learning: look closely into whatever is in front of you.
Wang Yangming’s term for the conscience everyone has before any study.
Literally, selected sayings: the collected conversations of Confucius and his students.

practices.name: Morning recitation
practices.instructions: Open the Analects at the next passage. Read it aloud twice, slowly. Copy one sentence of it by hand into a notebook, as neatly as you can. Under it write in a line what it asks of you today. Go through the book in order, a passage or two a day. When one seems dull or strange, copy it anyway.
practices.why: For two thousand years students in East Asia began the day by reciting the classics. Confucius called himself someone who loved learning more than anything.
variations: Learn one saying by heart each week.
Copy the passage with a brush, in Chinese or in your own script.
Read it with someone and argue about it for five minutes.

practices.name: Quiet sitting
practices.instructions: Sit upright on a chair or cushion with your hands resting on your knees and your eyes lowered. For ten minutes let the heart-mind settle. Do not chase thoughts and do not fight them. When the mind is clearer, bring up one relationship or duty that is waiting for you today and look at it calmly. End by standing and straightening your clothes.
practices.why: Later Confucians called this jingzuo. Zhu Xi advised half a day of reading and half a day of quiet sitting. Its purpose is to collect yourself so that you can act well.
variations: Sit after study, to let the passage sink in.
Sit outdoors, facing a tree or water.
Sit for five minutes before a hard conversation.

practices.name: Set yourself straight
practices.instructions: Before you meet anyone, set yourself in order: make the bed, wash, dress properly, and straighten your back. Look at yourself and say, quietly: I will be someone people can rely on today. The Analects says Confucius was always properly dressed and sat only on a mat that was straight. Good form begins with the body.
practices.why: Order outside helps order inside. Confucius paid close attention to how he dressed, sat and stood, as the Analects records. It is the first step of li, good form.
variations: Tidy your desk as well.
Stand tall for one minute.
Iron or brush one garment.

practices.name: Greet properly
practices.instructions: Greet each person at home, at work or in the street with a proper greeting: their name or title, good morning, a real question after them. Say thank you properly when you leave, and goodbye properly when you go. The first rule of this Onda is that you greet properly, thank properly and take your leave properly. Small forms make a warm day.
practices.why: Li, good form, is made of small things like greeting, thanking and leaving. The Analects treats them as the bones of a decent society.
variations: Greet everyone at home by name.
Greet the person who cleans or serves.
Say goodbye with a small bow.

practices.name: One new, one old
practices.instructions: Choose one new thing to learn today, a word, a fact, a skill, and one old thing to review: a lesson from last week, a vocabulary list, a piece of music. Write both on a card and keep it by you. In the evening, check them off. The Analects begins by praising learning and then going over it again with a glad heart.
practices.why: The opening line of the Analects is: to learn and in due time to review, is that not a joy? The rule of this Onda is to learn one thing today and review one thing.
variations: Use it to review the previous day.
Teach the new thing to someone.
Keep a running list.

practices.name: Pour tea for the household
practices.instructions: Make a pot of tea and pour a cup for each person at home, eldest first, holding the pot or cup with both hands. If you live alone, take a cup to a neighbour or colleague. Tea came into use centuries after Confucius and became the daily form of hospitality in China. Serve before you drink.
practices.why: Serving tea to others before yourself, with both hands, is a daily act of respect in China and across East Asia. It is gentle, pleasant and quick.
variations: Serve an elder and say nothing but thank you.
Learn how to warm the cups first.
Make it a morning custom.

practices.name: Tend one bond
practices.instructions: Each day do one concrete thing for one of your close relationships: a parent, a grandparent, a brother or sister, a teacher, an old friend. Call and ask about their day before you tell yours. Run the errand they have been putting off. Send the photograph they asked for. Choose a different person each day until you have been round the circle.
practices.why: Humaneness in this tradition begins at home and widens outward. Confucius said that filial devotion and respect between brothers and sisters are the root of goodness.
variations: Write a real letter to an elder.
Cook for your parents or for someone who stood in their place.
Ask an older relative for a story you have never heard.

practices.name: Set one name right
practices.instructions: Choose one thing in your life that you are calling by a name that is too kind: a lazy afternoon called rest, a lie called tact, a habit called fine. Write what it really is, in one plain word. Confucius said the first task of good government was to set names right. Do it for yourself, calmly, and then decide whether to act.
practices.why: Zhengming, the rectification of names, is the idea that clear speech is the root of clear action. It is among the sharpest of the Confucian practices.
variations: Do it for a job title.
Do it for a relationship.
Do it for a feeling.

practices.name: Correct yourself first
practices.instructions: Before you criticise anyone today, stop and ask: what is my part in this? Where have I fallen short in the same way? Write one line. Then decide whether the criticism is still needed, and how to say it kindly. The rule of this Onda is to correct yourself before you correct anyone. It makes you slower to blame and quicker to help.
practices.why: Confucius taught that the exemplary person looks within when things go wrong and the petty person looks to others. It is a hard rule and a very freeing one.
variations: Do it before a message you are angry about.
Do it for a child’s mistake.
Do it for your own mistake and forgive yourself.

practices.name: Put yourself in their place
practices.instructions: Pick someone you will deal with today and, before you meet, spend a minute imagining the day from their side: what they want, what they fear, what they have had to do. That is shu, reciprocity, the one word that Confucius said could guide a whole life. Then act in the way you would like it done to you.
practices.why: In the Analects, Zigong asks if there is one word to guide a life. Confucius answers shu: what you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.
variations: Do it for someone who irritates you.
Do it for a stranger on a bus.
Do it before every email today.

practices.name: A letter to a teacher
practices.instructions: Write a short letter of thanks to a teacher, living or not: someone who taught you something that has lasted. Say what they taught you, and what it has meant. Send it if you can. In East Asia the teacher is among the most honoured people, and the thanks are part of what makes a student. Do it while you remember.
practices.why: Respect for teachers is one of the abiding features of Confucian cultures. A teacher is honoured almost as a parent, and gratitude to them is a duty and a pleasure.
variations: Write to a teacher from long ago.
Write to someone who taught you outside school.
Say thank you in person.

practices.name: Write your best hand
practices.instructions: Copy one short sentence or a few characters in your very best handwriting, slowly, with a good pen. Sit up straight and let each stroke be careful. Calligraphy was one of the scholar’s arts, and handwriting was thought to show character. Hang or keep the page where you can see it, and see how it feels to do one small thing very well.
practices.why: In Chinese culture, writing is an art and a sign of the person. Careful handwriting is a modest, pleasant way to bring attention to something you do without thinking.
variations: Use a brush pen.
Write a line of a poem you like.
Write the same line three times and pick the best.

practices.name: The meal in good form
practices.instructions: Make one meal a day a small ceremony. Lay the table properly. Put the phone in another room. Serve the others before yourself, eldest and guests first. Wait until everyone is ready before you start. Eat at the pace of the slowest. Thank whoever cooked, and if you cooked, accept the thanks. Clear up together.
practices.why: Book 10 of the Analects records how Confucius ate, sat and received gifts: he did not eat what was badly cut, and did not sit on a mat that was not straight. Good form turns eating into respect.
variations: Pour tea for others before your own cup, holding it with both hands.
Invite someone to share a meal who rarely gets asked.
Learn the table manners of a guest’s culture before they come.

practices.name: Zengzi’s three questions
practices.instructions: Before bed, ask yourself the three questions that Confucius’s student Zengzi asked himself every day, and write a line in answer to each. In acting for others today, did I do my utmost? In dealing with friends, was I true to my word? Did I practise what was handed on to me? If the answer to one is no, write what you will do about it.
practices.why: Analects 1.4 gives this as Zengzi’s daily examination. It turns the day’s faults into tomorrow’s work and keeps self-cultivation practical.
variations: Ask the three questions aloud with a friend or partner.
Add a fourth: whom did I learn from today?
Read the week’s answers every seventh day.

practices.name: Review one thing
practices.instructions: Take the one thing you learned today, and go back over it. Say it aloud as if teaching it. Write a short summary, and one question. Notice what you have already forgotten, and what stuck. The Analects praises the one who reviews the old and so comes to understand the new. Fifteen minutes in the evening is enough to turn a day’s learning into something that lasts.
practices.why: Reviewing is half of learning in the Confucian tradition. The Analects says that one who reviews the old and knows the new is fit to be a teacher.
variations: Teach it to someone at home.
Write it as three flashcards.
Review last week’s thing as well.

practices.name: A scholar’s game
practices.instructions: Play a game of weiqi, Go, or xiangqi, Chinese chess, with someone or against a computer. They were two of the four arts of the scholar, with the zither, calligraphy and painting. Play slowly. Win or lose, shake hands and thank your opponent. Notice how a game can be both a contest and a courtesy.
practices.why: The four arts of the Chinese scholar were music, chess, calligraphy and painting. Playing a game with grace is a very Confucian pleasure.
variations: Play a quick game of touhu with a friend.
Play a handicap game with a beginner.
Study a famous game for ten minutes.

practices.name: Listen to the zither
practices.instructions: Play a piece for the guqin, the seven-stringed zither that scholars were expected to play, such as Flowing Water. Sit and do nothing else for ten minutes. Notice the pauses. The guqin was the instrument of the self-cultivated person, played alone or for a friend. Let the music be a form of quiet sitting.
practices.why: Music, with ritual, was one of the great concerns of Confucius. He held that music shapes character, and the guqin was seen as the instrument of the gentleman.
variations: Listen with a cup of tea.
Listen with your eyes closed.
Look up the story of the piece first.

practices.name: Be the same alone
practices.instructions: Before you go to bed, act as if someone you respect were watching you: tidy the room, put away what you left out, speak kindly to yourself. Shendu, being watchful when alone, is the Confucian test of sincerity: being the same person with no one there. Do one small thing you would do before a guest, and notice how it feels.
practices.why: The Great Learning says that the exemplary person is watchful over himself when alone. Sincerity means that your inside and outside are the same.
variations: Do it in the kitchen.
Do it before you check your phone.
Do it for a room no one sees.

practices.name: Visit an elder
practices.instructions: Visit an older relative, a neighbour or a former teacher in person, and give them a whole afternoon. Bring something small: fruit, tea, a flower. Sit with them, ask for stories, and help with anything they need. Do not look at your phone. In Confucian life, visiting elders is one of the main ways to show care. Leave when they are tired, and say you will come again.
practices.why: Filial devotion is the root of humaneness in Confucian thought. A visit, with time and attention, is the most direct way of showing it.
variations: Take a child with you.
Take a meal.
Ask them to teach you something.

practices.name: Make dumplings together
practices.instructions: Gather family or friends and make dumplings together: one rolls, one fills, one folds, one boils. Set a big table and talk while you work. This is the New Year task that puts three generations round one table with flour on their hands. Eat them together, hot, with a dipping sauce. It is the Confucian family at its best.
practices.why: Jiaozi, folded by the whole family for the Lunar New Year, are a meal and a ritual in one. Many hands, one table, and the eating in common are the point.
variations: Do it with a child learning to fold.
Make a double batch and give half away.
Ask each person to tell a family story as they fold.

immersePlan.name: Read a book of the Analects
immersePlan.text: Read one short book of the Analects in one sitting, such as Book 4 or Book 1. Choose a sentence, copy it, and write what it asks of you today.

immersePlan.name: Read Mencius on the child at the well
immersePlan.text: Read the passage in which Mencius says that anyone seeing a child about to fall into a well would feel alarm and pity. Ask whether he is right, and what that feeling is.

immersePlan.name: Read The Great Learning
immersePlan.text: Read the short text that moves from investigating things to a peaceful world, one step at a time. Notice where you are on its ladder, and which step you are skipping.

immersePlan.name: Watch Eat Drink Man Woman
immersePlan.text: Watch Ang Lee’s film about a widowed master chef in Taipei who cooks a banquet every Sunday for his three daughters. Notice what is said at the table, and what is not.

immersePlan.name: Watch Tokyo Story
immersePlan.text: Watch Ozu’s film of elderly parents visiting their grown children in the city and finding them busy. Notice the quiet. Ask whom you have not visited.

immersePlan.name: Watch A Simple Life
immersePlan.text: Watch Ann Hui’s film of a Hong Kong film producer looking after the servant who raised him when she falls ill. Notice what care looks like in small acts.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Flowing Water on the guqin
immersePlan.text: Play the piece for the seven-stringed zither that scholars were expected to play. Sit and do nothing else for ten minutes. Follow the pauses.

immersePlan.name: Listen to the Plum Blossom variations
immersePlan.text: Play the guqin piece in which the plum flowers in the cold. It is one of the best-loved pieces for the instrument. Notice how the same melody returns changed.

immersePlan.name: Hear Korean royal ancestral music
immersePlan.text: Play the slow court music of Korea, with bells, stone chimes and dance, performed for the ancestors. Listen with attention to the long gaps between sounds.

immersePlan.name: Look at The Classic of Filial Piety scroll
immersePlan.text: Look at the handscroll by Li Gonglin, pairing each chapter of the text with a quiet ink scene. Choose one scene and say what it asks.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Qingming scroll
immersePlan.text: Look at a section of the five-metre scroll of city life in which everyone has a place and a task. Find a person you would like to meet and say what they are doing.

immersePlan.name: Look at a portrait of Confucius
immersePlan.text: Look at the standard image of the Master, bowing slightly with hands clasped. Notice what the pose says. Try it for a moment, and see how it feels in the body.

immersePlan.name: Eat a meal in season, properly cut
immersePlan.text: Make a simple meal of rice, one vegetable and one dish, in season, with food cut neatly. The Analects says he did not eat what was out of season or badly cut. Eat slowly.

immersePlan.name: Eat a slice of ginger with the meal
immersePlan.text: Take a thin slice of fresh ginger with a meal. Book 10 of the Analects notes that he was never without ginger when he ate. Notice its warmth.

immersePlan.name: Make dumplings with someone
immersePlan.text: Fold dumplings with someone, roll, fill and pleat, and eat them hot together. It is the New Year task that puts three generations round one table.

immersePlan.name: Serve tea to an elder with both hands
immersePlan.text: Make tea and serve it to an older person with both hands, saying nothing but the offer. Tea became the daily form of hospitality in China.

immersePlan.name: Offer warm water to a guest
immersePlan.text: Offer a cup of plain hot water to anyone who comes in. It is the everyday drink in Chinese homes, offered to any guest on arrival. Drink one too.

immersePlan.name: Taste sweet fermented rice soup
immersePlan.text: The Analects says that only in wine he set himself no fixed limit, but never drank to confusion. If you prefer, try sweet fermented rice soup without alcohol. Take small sips and eat slowly.

immersePlan.name: Greet with joined hands
immersePlan.text: Greet someone today with hands clasped in front and a slight bend from the waist, a greeting between equals. Notice how it changes the moment.

immersePlan.name: Stand for a teacher
immersePlan.text: Rise when a teacher, mentor or elder comes into the room. In much of East Asia students stand when the teacher enters. Try it once with grace.

immersePlan.name: Tend a grave or a memory
immersePlan.text: At Qingming in early April families clean the graves of their ancestors. Visit a grave or tend a memory today: clean a stone, bring flowers, or tell a story about someone.

immersePlan.name: Play weiqi
immersePlan.text: Play a short game of Go, one of the four arts of the scholar with the zither, calligraphy and painting. Play on a small board with someone, and bow at the end.

immersePlan.name: Play touhu
immersePlan.text: Play pitch-pot: guests take turns throwing arrows into a narrow-necked vase. Use pencils and a tall jar. It is a party game of courtesy and good humour.

immersePlan.name: Play Chinese chess
immersePlan.text: Play xiangqi, Chinese chess, with two armies across a river and a general who stays in his palace. Learn the moves and play with someone.

immersePlan.name: Keep Confucius’s birthday
immersePlan.text: Confucius’s birthday on 28 September is kept as Teachers’ Day in Taiwan. Thank a teacher, in person or by letter, and read one passage of the Analects.

immersePlan.name: Mark the Lunar New Year
immersePlan.text: At Lunar New Year, everyone goes home, and younger people pay their respects to their elders. Call an elder today and wish them well in the new year.

immersePlan.name: Look up Qufu
immersePlan.text: Look up his home town in Shandong, with the temple, the family mansion and the forest cemetery. Read a short account of a visit and look at the cypresses.

immersePlan.name: Practise ren
immersePlan.text: Ren is humaneness, goodness toward others. Do one thing today that is simply kind and unnoticed, and say nothing about it.

immersePlan.name: Practise li
immersePlan.text: Li is good form, ritual. Choose one small ritual today, a greeting, a thank you, a leaving, and do it with full care.

immersePlan.name: Practise shu
immersePlan.text: Shu is reciprocity, putting yourself in another’s place. Before a conversation today, spend one minute imagining it from their side.

rules.text: Do not do to others what you would not want done to you
rules.why: Asked for a single word to act on for a whole life, Confucius answered reciprocity and explained it this way. Run each thing you do today past it.

rules.text: Greet properly, thank properly, take your leave properly
rules.why: Good form is how respect becomes visible. Look up, use the name and finish the sentence, with everyone you meet today.

rules.text: Correct yourself before you correct anyone
rules.why: On meeting someone unworthy, the Analects says, look inward and examine yourself. Each time you want to criticise today, find the same fault at home first.

rules.text: Call things by their right names
rules.why: When names are wrong, speech does not fit, and nothing gets done properly. Say late and not running behind; say no and not maybe.
At the door, at the table and in conversation. Yielding is practice in putting someone else at the centre.

rules.text: Learn one thing today and review one thing
rules.why: The first line of the Analects is about the pleasure of learning and of going back over it. Do both before you sleep.

read.title: The Analects
read.creator: Confucius, trans. Annping Chin
read.year: compiled about 5th to 3rd century BCE; this translation 2014
read.why: Five hundred short exchanges between a teacher and his students: jokes, rebukes, grief and advice. Read a few a day.

read.title: Mencius
read.creator: trans. D. C. Lau
read.why: The second founder argues with kings. Human nature is good, he says, and a ruler who starves his people has lost the right to rule.

read.title: Xunzi: The Complete Text
read.creator: trans. Eric L. Hutton
read.why: The tough-minded Confucian: people are born crooked like warped wood, and ritual and teachers are the steam and press that straighten them.

read.title: The Great Learning and The Doctrine of the Mean
read.creator: trans. Andrew Plaks
read.why: Two short chapters from the Book of Rites that became core texts. The first sets out the path from self-cultivation to peace in the world on a single page.

read.title: Confucius: The Secular as Sacred
read.creator: Herbert Fingarette
read.why: A small, startling book by an American philosopher on why a handshake is a kind of holy rite.

read.title: Confucius and the World He Created
read.creator: Michael Schuman
read.why: The life, the long afterlife and the modern revival, told by a journalist who married into a Korean family.

read.title: The Story of the Stone
read.creator: Cao Xueqin, trans. David Hawkes
read.why: Also called Dream of the Red Chamber. The greatest Chinese novel shows a large Confucian household from inside, with all its rules and those who suffer under them.

watch.title: Confucius
watch.creator: Hu Mei
watch.why: A large-scale film biography with Chow Yun-fat, covering the years in office and the long wandering. Reverent, and good on the setting.

watch.title: Eat Drink Man Woman
watch.creator: Ang Lee
watch.why: A widowed master chef in Taipei cooks a banquet every Sunday for three daughters who are trying to leave. Duty, food and what goes unsaid.

watch.title: Tokyo Story
watch.creator: Yasujirō Ozu
watch.why: Elderly parents visit their grown children in the city and find them busy. The most quietly devastating film about filial duty.

watch.title: A Simple Life
watch.creator: Ann Hui
watch.why: A Hong Kong film producer looks after the servant who raised him when she has a stroke. Devotion that runs the other way.

watch.title: The Farewell
watch.creator: Lulu Wang
watch.why: A family hides a grandmother’s diagnosis from her and stages a wedding so that everyone can say goodbye. A Chinese American granddaughter struggles with the lie.

listen.title: Flowing Water
listen.creator: Guan Pinghu, guqin
listen.why: A piece for the seven-stringed zither that scholars were expected to play. This recording was sent into space on the Voyager spacecraft in 1977.

listen.title: Three Variations on the Plum Blossom
listen.creator: Traditional, guqin
listen.why: The plum flowers in the cold. One of the best-loved pieces for the instrument, on steadfastness.

listen.title: Jongmyo Jeryeak
listen.creator: Royal ancestral rite music of Korea
listen.why: Slow court music with bells, stone chimes and dance, performed for the spirits of the Joseon kings and still played in Seoul each May.

listen.title: Confucian temple music
listen.creator: Performed at the autumn rite in Taipei and Qufu
listen.why: Austere music for bronze bells, stone chimes, flutes and drums, with one note to each word of the hymn.

art.title: The Classic of Filial Piety
art.creator: Li Gonglin
art.why: A handscroll that pairs each chapter of the text with a quiet ink scene of family life. Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.

art.title: Along the River During the Qingming Festival
art.creator: Zhang Zeduan
art.why: Five metres of city life in which everyone has a place and a task, from boatmen to scholars. Palace Museum, Beijing.

art.title: Draft of a Requiem to My Nephew
art.creator: Yan Zhenqing
art.why: A loyal official’s grief for a murdered nephew, with the crossings-out left in. Calligraphy read as a portrait of character. National Palace Museum, Taipei.

art.title: The Kaicheng Stone Classics
art.creator: Carved under the Tang dynasty
art.why: The Confucian classics cut into 114 stone slabs so that no copyist could corrupt them. Forest of Steles, Xi’an.

art.title: Portrait of Confucius
art.creator: After Wu Daozi, stone rubbing
art.why: The standard image of the Master, bowing slightly with hands clasped. Rubbings are taken from a stone at Qufu.

eat.title: A meal in season, properly cut
eat.creator: Rice, one vegetable, one dish of meat or tofu
eat.why: The Analects says he did not eat food out of season or badly cut, or without its proper sauce. Cook simply and with care.

eat.title: Ginger
eat.creator: A slice with the meal
eat.why: Book 10 notes that he was never without ginger when he ate.

eat.title: Dumplings made together
eat.creator: Jiaozi, filled and folded by the whole family
eat.why: The New Year task that puts three generations round one table with flour on their hands.

eat.title: Millet or rice porridge
eat.creator: Plain, with pickles
eat.why: The everyday grain of north China in his time. Coarse rice and water to drink, he said, and joy is to be found in the midst of these.

drink.title: Tea served to an elder
drink.creator: Offered with both hands
drink.why: Tea came into use centuries after Confucius and became the daily form of respect he would have recognised.

drink.title: Warm water
drink.creator: Plain and hot
drink.why: The everyday drink in Chinese homes, offered to any guest on arrival.

drink.title: Rice wine in moderation
drink.creator: Or sweet fermented rice soup without alcohol
drink.why: Only in wine did he set himself no fixed limit, the Analects says, and he never drank to confusion.

customs.title: The bow with joined hands
customs.creator: A greeting between equals
customs.why: Hands clasped in front and a slight bend from the waist. Still used at New Year and at ceremonies.

customs.title: Standing for a teacher
customs.creator: Respect for the one who teaches
customs.why: Students rise when the teacher enters. In much of East Asia a teacher is honoured for life.

customs.title: Sweeping the tombs
customs.creator: At Qingming in early April
customs.why: Families clean the graves of their ancestors, set out food and report the year’s news.

customs.title: The capping ceremony
customs.creator: Coming of age
customs.why: At twenty a young man was given a cap and an adult name, and a young woman had her hair pinned up at fifteen. From then on they answered for themselves.

games.title: Weiqi
games.creator: Board game · China
games.why: One of the four arts of the scholar, with the zither, calligraphy and painting. Confucius remarked that playing it was at least better than doing nothing.

games.title: Touhu
games.creator: Party game · China
games.why: Pitch-pot: guests take turns throwing arrows into a narrow-necked vase, and the loser drinks. The Book of Rites has a whole chapter on doing it politely.

games.title: Xiangqi
games.creator: Board game · China
games.year: current form since the Song dynasty
games.why: Chinese chess, played in every park. The general stays in his palace with his advisers, which is a small lesson in itself.

games.title: Emperor: Rise of the Middle Kingdom
games.creator: Video game · BreakAway Games
games.why: A city builder set across early Chinese history. Your people need ancestral shrines and academies, and Confucius can be invited to visit.

festivals.title: Confucius’s birthday
festivals.creator: 28 September
festivals.why: Kept as Teachers’ Day in Taiwan. A dawn rite with music and rows of dancers holding pheasant feathers is performed at Confucian temples, and in Qufu by his descendants.

festivals.title: Qingming
festivals.creator: Early April
festivals.why: Tomb-sweeping day. The yearly act of filial devotion toward those who came before.

festivals.title: Lunar New Year
festivals.creator: Late January or February
festivals.why: Everyone goes home. Younger people pay respects to their elders and receive red envelopes in return.

festivals.title: Seokjeon Daeje
festivals.creator: Spring and autumn, Seoul
festivals.why: The full rite to Confucius as it has been kept at Sungkyunkwan since the fifteenth century, with court music and dance.

festivals.title: Double Ninth
festivals.creator: 9th day of the ninth lunar month
festivals.why: Kept in China as a day for honouring older people.

places.title: Qufu
places.creator: Shandong, China
places.why: His home town. The temple, the family mansion and the forest cemetery where he and more than seventy generations of his descendants are buried form a World Heritage Site.

places.title: Temple of Confucius and Imperial Academy
places.creator: Beijing, China
places.why: Courtyards of old cypresses and 198 stone tablets carved with the names of everyone who passed the highest examination over six centuries.

places.title: Temple of Literature
places.creator: Hanoi, Vietnam
places.why: Founded in 1070, with Vietnam’s first university. Stone tablets on the backs of tortoises list its graduates.

places.title: Sungkyunkwan
places.creator: Seoul, South Korea
places.why: The royal Confucian academy of 1398, with a shrine and lecture hall under ginkgo trees, in the grounds of a modern university.

places.title: Yuelu Academy
places.creator: Changsha, Hunan, China
places.why: A school founded in 976 where Zhu Xi lectured. It has been a place of teaching for more than a thousand years.

places.title: Taipei Confucius Temple
places.creator: Taipei, Taiwan
places.why: A plain southern-style temple without statues, known for its dawn rite on 28 September.

ethics.title: Humaneness
ethics.text: Ren is the feeling for others that makes a person fully a person. Confucius gave different answers every time he was asked what it was, because it shows itself differently with each person in front of you.
ethics.practice: Give one person today your complete attention for as long as they are speaking.

ethics.title: Reciprocity
ethics.text: The measure is close to hand: your own likes and dislikes. What you would hate to receive, do not hand out. Confucius called this the one thread that ran through all his teaching.
ethics.practice: Before sending a message today, read it as the person receiving it.

ethics.title: Filial devotion
ethics.text: Care for parents is where a child first learns to put someone else first. It includes respect as well as support: even dogs and horses are fed, the Analects says.
ethics.practice: Do something for a parent or elder today, and do it with a good face.

ethics.title: Rightness before profit
ethics.text: The exemplary person asks what is right. The petty person asks what there is to gain. Wealth and rank are welcome when they come the right way and otherwise are floating clouds.
ethics.practice: Find one choice today where the right thing costs you something, and make it.

ethics.title: Gentle remonstrance
ethics.text: Loyalty is not silence. A child should correct a parent, softly, and a minister should tell a ruler the truth. If you are not heeded, stay respectful and do not give up.
ethics.practice: Raise one concern today with someone senior to you, with care for how you say it.

ethics.title: Faults seen and mended
ethics.text: To have faults and not correct them, that is the real fault. The exemplary person’s errors are like an eclipse: everyone sees them, and everyone looks up when they pass.
ethics.practice: Admit one mistake today to the person it affected, and put it right.

philosophy.title: Ritual makes us human
philosophy.text: A greeting, a shared meal or a funeral done properly is more than etiquette. In performing it together people become present to each other. Without form, Confucius said, respect turns to fuss and courage to disorder.
philosophy.practice: Choose one small daily exchange, such as a greeting or a handing over, and perform it today with full care.

philosophy.title: Learning as joy
philosophy.text: The first line of the Analects is about the pleasure of studying and practising. Learning here means becoming someone, and it never finishes. Confucius described himself as so eager that he forgot to eat.
philosophy.practice: Spend twenty minutes today on something difficult for its own sake.

philosophy.title: Are we born good?
philosophy.text: Mencius said that anyone who sees a child about to fall into a well feels alarm, and that this is the sprout of goodness. Xunzi said that our nature is selfish and that goodness is made by effort. Both agreed that it takes cultivation.
philosophy.practice: Notice your first unplanned response to someone in trouble today. Then decide what to grow from it.

philosophy.title: Setting names right
philosophy.text: Asked what he would do first in government, Confucius said: correct the names. If words do not match things, instructions cannot be carried out and people do not know where to put hand or foot.
philosophy.practice: Find one word you use to hide something from yourself. Replace it with the accurate one.

philosophy.title: Harmony, not sameness
philosophy.text: The exemplary person harmonises without agreeing for the sake of it, and the petty person agrees without harmony. The image is cooking: a good soup needs different flavours in balance.
philosophy.practice: In one discussion today, add the view that is missing, without turning it into a fight.

philosophy.title: Ruling by character
philosophy.text: Govern by virtue, the Analects says, and you are like the North Star, which stays in its place while the other stars turn toward it. Lead by punishment and people only learn to avoid being caught.
philosophy.practice: Wherever you are in charge today, do first what you want others to do.

philosophy.title: The widening circle
philosophy.text: The Great Learning sets out a chain: to bring peace to the world, first order the state; to do that, first put the family right; to do that, first cultivate yourself; and to do that, set the heart straight and look into things.
philosophy.practice: Pick the innermost circle that is out of order and work on that one today.

philosophy.title: Knowing and doing are one
philosophy.text: Wang Yangming held that if you really know a thing is good, you are already doing it, and that knowledge which does not act is not yet knowledge.
philosophy.practice: Take one thing you know you should do and do it within the hour.

journal: In acting for others today, did you do your utmost?
Were you true to your word with your friends?
Did you practise what you have been taught?
Whom did you learn from today, and what?
What did you do today that you would not want done to you?
Which relationship did you tend, and which did you neglect?
Where did good form make something easier?
What did you call by the wrong name?
When did you think of gain before you thought of what was right?
What fault did you see in someone that is also yours?
How did you treat the oldest person you met today?

Where did you agree in order to avoid trouble?
What would your teacher say about today?
How do you behave when no one is watching?
What do you owe your parents that cannot be repaid?
Which mistake did you admit, and which did you cover?
Who looks to you as an example, and what did they see?
What was the most carefully done thing in your day?
When did you go first when you should have yielded?
What did you study for the joy of it?
What would it mean to be the same person at home, at work and alone?

Which relationship changed in these days, and how?
Where did good form free you, and where did it feel empty?
What have you learned by heart that you will keep?
What kind of ancestor do you want to be?
Which practice will you carry on?

intro: Confucianism is a way of becoming a good person among other people. It has no creator god and no church. Its sacred ground is the family table, the schoolroom and the public office, and its question is a practical one: how should we treat one another so that a household, and then a country, can live in peace?

The man at its source was Kong Qiu, known in China as Kongzi, Master Kong. He was born in 551 BCE in the small state of Lu, in a period when the old Zhou order was breaking down into war between rival lords. He was poor, largely self-taught and convinced that the remedy lay in the past: in the humane government and careful rites of the early Zhou kings. He hoped to advise a ruler. He held office briefly, spent some fourteen years on the road looking for a prince who would listen, and found none. He returned home to teach, and died thinking he had failed.

His students remembered what he said. The Analects, compiled over the generations after his death, records him in fragments: answering the same question differently for different pupils, mourning his favourite student, joking and losing his temper. He claimed to invent nothing. He said he was a transmitter who loved the ancients. What he passed on was a picture of the exemplary person, the junzi, made by long study and practice and not by birth.

The teaching rests on a few words. Ren is humaneness, the feeling for others that makes us fully human. Li is ritual or good form, the shared shapes through which respect is shown, from a state sacrifice to the way a cup is handed over. Xiao is the devotion of children to parents, where everyone first learns to care for someone. Shu is reciprocity: do not do to others what you would not want for yourself. Goodness starts in the nearest relationships and widens from there.

Later thinkers argued over the foundations. Mencius held that people are born with the sprouts of goodness. Xunzi held that they are born selfish and are straightened by teaching. Under the Han dynasty the school became the creed of the state, and for most of the next two thousand years anyone who wanted to hold office in China had to master its books. Korea, Japan and Vietnam built their own versions. Zhu Xi in the twelfth century and Wang Yangming in the sixteenth renewed it as a discipline of the inner life.

That long alliance with power has a cost. Confucian language was used to demand obedience from subjects, from the young and above all from women, and reformers in the twentieth century attacked it for exactly this. The tradition also holds its own corrective: the duty to remonstrate, and the teaching of Mencius that a ruler who abuses the people is a ruler no longer. In this Onda you will study each morning, sit quietly, look after one relationship a day, eat one meal with care and examine yourself at night.
guide.origin: The state of Lu, in what is now Shandong, China. The tradition spread to Korea, Japan and Vietnam
guide.era: Confucius lived from 551 to 479 BCE. His school has shaped East Asia for some 2,500 years

figures.name: Confucius (Kong Qiu)
figures.bio: Teacher from the state of Lu. He held minor office, wandered for years in search of a ruler to advise and went home to teach. He said he transmitted and did not create.

figures.name: Yan Hui
figures.bio: His favourite student, poor and tireless, who could hear one point and grasp ten. When he died young, Confucius cried out that Heaven was destroying him.

figures.name: Zengzi
figures.bio: The student who examined himself on three points daily. He is linked with the teaching of filial devotion and with the Great Learning.

figures.name: Mencius (Meng Ke)
figures.bio: The second sage. He argued before kings that human nature is good and that the people matter most, the state next and the ruler least.

figures.name: Xunzi (Xun Kuang)
figures.bio: The realist. He taught that goodness is the product of deliberate effort and ritual, and he wrote the first sustained essays in Chinese philosophy.

figures.name: Dong Zhongshu
figures.bio: The Han scholar who persuaded Emperor Wu to favour Confucian learning and tied it to a theory of Heaven, earth and humankind.

figures.name: Ban Zhao
figures.bio: Historian who completed the official history of the Han and taught the empress. Her Lessons for Women argued that girls should be educated, within the limits of her age.

figures.name: Han Yu
figures.bio: Tang essayist who defended the Confucian Way against Buddhism and was exiled for it. He set off the revival that followed.

figures.name: Zhu Xi
figures.bio: The great synthesiser. He chose the Four Books, wrote the commentaries that every examination candidate memorised for six centuries, and made self-cultivation a daily method.

figures.name: Wang Yangming
figures.bio: General, governor and philosopher. He taught that everyone has inborn moral knowing and that knowing and acting are one thing.

figures.name: Yi Hwang (Toegye)
figures.bio: Korea’s foremost Confucian thinker, who founded an academy and wrote Ten Diagrams on Sage Learning for a young king. His portrait is on the 1,000 won note.

figures.name: Tu Weiming
figures.bio: Scholar at Harvard and Peking universities who has presented Confucianism to the modern world as a living, self-critical humanism.

history.detail: He was born at Qufu in the state of Lu. His father, an old soldier, died when he was a small child, and he grew up poor.
After a short time in office he left Lu and travelled from state to state with a band of students, offering advice no ruler took. He was at times hungry, mocked and in danger.
He died at seventy-two, having spent his last years teaching and editing the old texts. His students mourned him for three years, as they would a father.
Two thinkers built opposing accounts of human nature on the same foundation and argued the school’s case against Mohists, Taoists and Legalists.
The First Emperor of Qin ordered private copies of the classics destroyed. Later tradition adds that hundreds of scholars were executed. The texts survived in hidden copies and in memory.
The Han court set up official posts for experts in the Five Classics, followed by an imperial academy in 124 BCE. Confucian learning became the road to office.
The Sui dynasty began to choose officials by written examination. Under the Tang and Song the system grew into the main gate to a career, open in principle to any man who could study.

history.what: Zhu Xi publishes the Four Books
history.detail: He gathered the Analects, the Mencius, the Great Learning and the Doctrine of the Mean with his commentaries as the core of education.
The Yuan court made his commentaries the basis of the examinations. They stayed so in China for almost six hundred years, and shaped Korea and Japan.
A new Korean dynasty made Neo-Confucianism the basis of the state. Korea became, by many measures, the most thoroughly Confucian society in history.
Jesuit missionaries published a Latin translation of three of the Four Books in Paris. The Latin name Confucius, from Kong Fuzi, dates from their work. Leibniz and Voltaire read it with admiration.
The Qing court ended the system after some thirteen centuries. The class of scholar-officials lost its purpose overnight.
Students and writers blamed the old teaching for China’s weakness and for the oppression of women and the young, and called for science and democracy in its place.
Red Guards smashed the temple and graves at Qufu in 1966. A national campaign in 1973 and 1974 denounced Confucius by name.
Temples were restored, the birthday rite returned to Qufu and the classics came back into schools. In 2004 China began to name its cultural institutes abroad after Confucius.

concepts.detail: The highest virtue and the hardest to pin down. It begins as love within the family and extends outward. Confucius would rarely grant that anyone had achieved it, and yet he said it is at hand the moment you truly want it.

The inherited forms for acting together: ceremonies, manners, dress, music. For Confucians these are the means by which feeling is trained and expressed, and by which a group becomes a community. Form without feeling is empty, and so is feeling without form.

The aim of all the training. Such a person is calm, generous, exacting with himself and easy on others, and cannot be used as a tool. The word once meant nobleman. Confucius made it a matter of character.

Children owe parents care, respect and, after death, remembrance. It is treated as the root from which wider goodness grows. Critics note that it has been used to demand obedience. The texts themselves allow, and require, respectful disagreement.

Parent and child, ruler and minister, husband and wife, older and younger, friend and friend. Each side has obligations to the other. Four of the five are unequal, and that inequality is what modern Confucians debate most.

Heaven grants the right to rule to the virtuous and withdraws it from tyrants. Floods, famines and rebellions were read as signs. Mencius drew the conclusion that killing a tyrant is not the killing of a king.
Social roles are names that carry duties. If a ruler does not behave as a ruler, the name is false and everything built on it goes wrong. Good order starts with honest language.

Mencius held that compassion, shame, deference and the sense of right and wrong are present in everyone like shoots. Tended, they grow into humaneness, rightness, good form and wisdom. Neglected, they wither.
Staying centred so that joy, anger, grief and pleasure arise in due measure. It is a practical skill and has nothing to do with being lukewarm.

Study, reflection, ritual practice and daily self-examination, pursued until right action becomes second nature. The Great Learning makes it the starting point of peace in the family, the state and the world.

facts.text: The name Confucius is a Latin form of Kong Fuzi, Master Kong, made by Jesuit missionaries in the seventeenth century.
His family tree is among the longest ever recorded. The edition completed in 2009 lists more than two million descendants across some eighty generations.
A gatekeeper in the Analects sums him up in one line: is he not the one who knows it cannot be done and keeps on doing it?
The imperial examinations ran for about 1,300 years. Candidates were locked into small brick cells for days with their brushes, food and bedding.
A recording of the zither piece Flowing Water, an emblem of the scholar’s art, was placed on the two Voyager spacecraft in 1977.
In the Analects Confucius says that at dinner only his wine had no fixed limit, though he never let it confuse him.
Stone tablets on the backs of 82 stone tortoises at the Temple of Literature in Hanoi list the graduates of royal examinations held between 1442 and 1779.

sensitivity.note: Confucianism is a living tradition for hundreds of millions of people in China, Korea, Japan, Vietnam and their diasporas, and it means different things in each place. It has also been used by rulers to demand obedience, and by families to subordinate women and the young. This Onda presents its ethics of learning, care and good form, and names the criticism.
requiredCaveats: There is no single Confucianism. The teaching of the Analects, the state creed of the empires and modern family custom are related and are not the same.
Hierarchy is built into most of the traditional relationships. Many modern Confucians argue for reading them as mutual duties between equals.
Filial devotion does not mean enduring harm. Nothing here asks you to stay in or return to an abusive relationship.
The temple rites belong to their communities. This Onda asks you to learn about them, not to imitate them.
This content has not yet been reviewed by scholars of the tradition or by people raised in it. It should be before release.
